title: Arranging off records: Red Nichols copy and Ellington's altered chords
summary: After Paschal takes over King's band, Levy is hired as banjoist and arranger. He copies a Red Nichols record arrangement, then works out Ellington's altered chords from records.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: How long did you have the Harman's?

Well, let me see, two, three years or something. Is that so? Yeah. You followed Cook? Followed Cook, yeah. That's right. Cook went to White City, that's right. I see. And then after King came out, I don't know what happened to the planet King, what he did or anything, but…
He went to Europe, you know.

That's right, he went to Europe, that's right. He went to Europe and the next year, Paschal, who used to play with Henderson. Paschal came in, Paschal got the band, he hired me as banjoist and ranger. Oh, I had made some arrangements for King's band, and incidentally, this might seem humorous, one of the boys came up to me and said, have you heard Red Nichols and Biff Moe play Ida, Sweeties Appleside? I said, yeah, I got the record. He said, why don't you steal that arrangement, arranging for the band. I said, what? Don't insult me. Steal it, arrange that off the record? I said, I wouldn't do anything like that. What are you talking about? I got mad. About two weeks later, I made the arrangement. Brought it to rehearsal and that boy, just like they played it and we played it, just like that. All the kids said, oh we know where that's from, that's from Red Nichols, Biff Moe's record. And so that started me to, when you couldn't get the arrangement, they'd say, Charlie, get that and get your record, let's play that. And then, and then, and then, Singing the Blues. Singing the Blues, I did the same thing, Singing the Blues, yeah, arrange that. And I laugh about that many times because, I'll tell you when Duke first came out with those five saxophones, I think, and we was playing at that, oh it's a copy club, man. And they used to play on the radio, you remember, what was it, six o'clock or something, they had a broadcast? I was glued to the radio. I was waiting for them to open up. And so, when he added, I was telling Mikey, when he added those extra saxophones, I began to hear some chords, I said, what is that chord? He's using, what is that? And, I said, what is that? It was by tonality, but I didn't know it then. See, one chord was in one key, and the other rest of the chord was in another key. So, I said, now I know what I'm going to do. I said, I'm going to go and buy those records, bring them home. I bought the records, bought seven dollars, had a whole load of the records, they had seven and a half, bought them all Duke's records, bought them home, and put the, I had a portable, phonograph with a photograph, right up by the piano, and I sat down at the piano and played with the thing. And I found out that he was taking the G7 chord, raising the fifth, lowering the fifth, putting a minor ninth in there, which gives three tones of the D flat chord, D flat, F, A, A flat, which is a D flat major chord, and that would fit right in, that's a lowered fifth of a G7, and a raised fifth of a G7, and a minor ninth in there. And that, now, later on I found this by tonality, but I said, well, that's what you call a triple altered chord. In the harmony books, we had to call it altered chords. When you raised a lowered one tone of the original chord, you call it an altered chord. So I knew enough of music, you know, and I said, oh, and I started making some arrangements. So I went around on the north side and peddled some of the arrangements, you know. And I had quite a kick out of it. Who just had your arrangements? Oh, yeah, Elmer Kaiser. Did you? I arranged for him about seven years. He had a very progressive band for a time, yes.
